svchost.exe masquerade written/executed outside System32 (N-central post-compromise) AIInstallation High
Hunts the N-central intrusion IOC where attackers drop a file named svchost.exe into a user's Documents folder (or any non-System32 path) on managed endpoints reached via Take Control. Legitimate svchost.exe only ever lives in System32/SysWOW64, so a copy elsewhere is a high-fidelity masquerade. Rationale: Uses the exact N-able-published IOC 'svchost.exe in users' Documents folders'. The System32/SysWOW64/WinSxS exclusion turns the OS's most-trusted binary name into a clean masquerade signal; second-sourced by N-able advisory + Huntress rapid-response. Cross-checked against: • https://www.n-able.com/blog/n-central-security-update-august-1-2026 • https://www.huntress.com/blog/n-able-vulnerability-exploitation • https://status.n-able.com/2026/08/02/n-central-2026-3-hotfix-1-mitigation-for-cve-2026-18577/
ATT&CKT1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Software installers/updaters that stage a bundled svchost.exe copy in %TEMP% or a program folder
  • Malware-analysis or IR sandboxes deliberately copying svchost.exe for testing
  • Backup/imaging tools writing shadow copies of Windows files to a staging directory
  • Developer debug symbols or driver packages extracting a System32 mirror to a non-standard path
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msiexec.exe","setup.exe","trustedinstaller.exe") and FolderPath !contains "\\Package Cache\\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full path, SHA256, and InitiatingProcess for the svchost.exe write; hash-check against the legitimate System32 svchost.exe — a mismatch or unsigned binary confirms masquerade. Note whether the host is an N-central-managed endpoint. 2) Contain: isolate the endpoint in Defender/EDR, kill any running process from the non-System32 path, and quarantine the file. 3) Hunt: on the same host and other endpoints under the same N-central/MSP account, look for a 'Cloudflared' service, Take Control (ui_access_control.log / BASupSrvc_*.log.gz) sessions, and outbound traffic to the published attacker IPs/domains.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "svchost.exe"
| where FolderPath !startswith @"C:\Windows\System32" and FolderPath !startswith @"C:\Windows\SysWOW64" and FolderPath !startswith @"C:\Windows\WinSxS"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "svchost.exe"
| where TargetFilePath !startswith @"C:\Windows\System32" and TargetFilePath !startswith @"C:\Windows\SysWOW64" and TargetFilePath !startswith @"C:\Windows\WinSxS"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername, TargetFileSHA256
title: svchost.exe Present Outside System32 (N-central Intrusion IOC)
id: 6f2d8b3a-1c4e-4b9a-9e7d-3a2f5c8e1b04
description: Detects a file named svchost.exe created outside legitimate Windows system directories, matching the N-able N-central post-compromise masquerade IOC (svchost.exe in users' Documents folders).
references:

  condition: selection and not filter_legit

source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @TargetFilename:(*\svchost.exe OR *\SVCHOST.EXE OR *\Svchost.exe) -@TargetFilename:(*\System32\* OR *\system32\* OR *\SysWOW64\* OR *\syswow64\* OR *\WinSxS\* OR *\winsxs\*)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten TargetFileName=/\\svchost\.exe$/i
| NOT (TargetFileName=/\\(System32|SysWOW64|WinSxS)\\/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, TargetFileName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())

Cloudflared registered as a Windows service for reboot-persistent tunneling AIInstallation High
Hunts the N-central post-compromise persistence step: attackers install cloudflared as a Windows service (named 'Cloudflared') on managed endpoints so an outbound Cloudflare tunnel survives reboot and outlives revocation of the N-central route. Targets the service-install / execution rather than generic quick-tunnel usage. Rationale: Uses the N-able-published IOC 'a service named Cloudflared' plus the disclosed persistence mechanism (tunnel-as-service surviving reboot/route revocation). Deliberately targets service-install/token args rather than duplicating the existing SigmaHQ generic cloudflared quick-tunnel and argotunnel-DNS rules; Sigma left blank for that reason. Cross-checked against: • https://www.n-able.com/blog/n-central-security-update-august-1-2026 • https://www.huntress.com/blog/n-able-vulnerability-exploitation • https://github.com/SigmaHQ/sigma/blob/master/rules/windows/process_creation/proc_creation_win_cloudflared_tunnel_run.yml
ATT&CKT1543.003 T1572
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Services
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT/MSP legitimately using Cloudflare Tunnel (cloudflared) for sanctioned remote access to a server
  • Developer running `cloudflared tunnel run` for local app testing
  • Sanctioned cloudflared service deployed by a network team on a jump host
  • Security tooling wrapping cloudflared for approved zero-trust access
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("svc-cloudflare","it-admin") and FolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files\cloudflared"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether Cloudflare Tunnel is sanctioned software for this host/customer; inspect the cloudflared install path, the --token/tunnel args, and the parent process (services.exe parent = reboot-persistent service = higher concern). 2) Contain: stop and disable the Cloudflared service, isolate the endpoint, and revoke/rotate the tunnel token with Cloudflare if it's your account (it is not — attacker-controlled, so block the tunnel egress at the firewall). 3) Hunt: enumerate all endpoints under the same N-central/MSP account for a Cloudflared service, an svchost.exe in Documents, and Take Control sessions tied to mspsupport@n-able.com.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "cloudflared.exe" or (ProcessCommandLine has "cloudflared" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("tunnel run","service install","--token","tunnel"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, ParentProcess = InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID in (4697, 7045)
| where ServiceName has "cloudflared" or ServiceFileName has "cloudflared"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account = SubjectUserName, ServiceName, ServiceFileName, ServiceStartType, ServiceType
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\cloudflared.exe OR *\Cloudflared.exe OR *\CLOUDFLARED.EXE) @CommandLine:(*tunnel* OR *"service install"* OR *--token*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\cloudflared\.exe$/i
| CommandLine=/(tunnel\s+run|service\s+install|--token|tunnel)/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, CommandLine, ParentBaseFileName], function=count())
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name="cloudflared.exe" OR Processes.process="*cloudflared*") AND Processes.process IN ("*tunnel run*","*service install*","*--token*","*tunnel*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name="cloudflared.exe" OR Processes.process="*cloudflared*") AND Processes.process IN ("*tunnel run*","*service install*","*--token*","*tunnel*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
Endpoint C2 to N-central attacker Synology QuickConnect domains / published IPs AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts outbound connections from managed endpoints to the specific infrastructure Huntress and N-able tied to the N-central intrusion: three Synology QuickConnect/DDNS domains and six published IPs (four confirmed Mullvad/NordVPN exit nodes). Article-specific IOC match, distinct from generic argotunnel-domain rules. Rationale: Uses the exact Huntress-published attacker domains and N-able's six published IPs. Huntress flagged four IPs as Mullvad/NordVPN exit nodes (hence Medium confidence / medium FP on the IP arm); the three QuickConnect domains are high-fidelity, so the DNS/domain arm is the primary signal. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/n-able-vulnerability-exploitation • https://www.n-able.com/blog/n-central-security-update-august-1-2026
ATT&CKT1572 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A user or server legitimately using Mullvad/NordVPN, whose exit node overlaps one of the four VPN-node IPs
  • Legitimate Synology NAS owners in the org reaching their own QuickConnect address (different subdomain, but analysts may confuse the pattern)
  • Threat-intel or sandbox appliance deliberately beaconing to these IOCs for validation
  • Shared-hosting IP reuse where a published IP is later reassigned to a benign service
Suppression filter
// Raise fidelity: require an on-host corroborator alongside a VPN-node IP match
| where RemoteUrl in~ ("mousears.synology.me","wagoosh.direct.quickconnect.to","who-ripped-one.direct.quickconnect.to") or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("cloudflared.exe","svchost.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process and account for the connection; a match on one of the three QuickConnect domains is high-fidelity, while an IP-only match against a VPN-node IP needs corroboration (pair with a Cloudflared service or svchost masquerade on the same host). 2) Contain: block the domains/IPs at egress, isolate matching endpoints, and capture the initiating binary. 3) Hunt: across all endpoints under the affected N-central/MSP account, pivot on the same domains/IPs, cloudflared service persistence, and Take Control session logs; confirm N-central is on build 2026.3.1.7.
let c2Domains = dynamic(["mousears.synology.me","wagoosh.direct.quickconnect.to","who-ripped-one.direct.quickconnect.to"]);
let c2IPs = dynamic(["173.249.252.200","87.249.138.34","37.19.210.32","37.153.90.88","92.118.112.181","68.235.46.214"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in (c2IPs) or RemoteUrl in~ (c2Domains)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
let c2Domains = dynamic(["mousears.synology.me","wagoosh.direct.quickconnect.to","who-ripped-one.direct.quickconnect.to"]);
let c2IPs = dynamic(["173.249.252.200","87.249.138.34","37.19.210.32","37.153.90.88","92.118.112.181","68.235.46.214"]);
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr in (c2IPs) or DstDomain in~ (c2Domains) or Url has_any (c2Domains)
| project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstDomain, DstPortNumber, Url, DvcHostname

ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:

level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name

Hugging Face Diffusers Flaws Could Let Model Repositories Execute Arbitrary Code

The Hacker News
2026-08-03 11 use cases 4 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

Three high-severity security flaws have been disclosed in Hugging Face's Diffusers library that could allow crafted model repositories to stealthily execute arbitrary code on machines that load it, opening the artificial intelligence (AI) supply chain to security risk. "These vulnerabilities are bypassing trust_remote_code, the safeguard designed to stop unreviewed code from running in the

FaceHugger: malicious custom-pipeline .py (incl. None.py) written into Hugging Face model cache AIDelivery High
Hunts for Python code files landing inside the Hugging Face hub/module cache in locations a legitimate diffusion model never ships them: a file literally named None.py (CVE-2026-44827), or any *.py under component subdirectories (unet/, scheduler/, vae/, text_encoder/, safety_checker/, feature_extractor/) or the diffusers_modules dynamic-import cache. These artifacts are the on-disk footprint of a crafted repo bypassing trust_remote_code during DiffusionPipeline.from_pretrained(). Rationale: Anchored on the article's explicit workaround guidance (inspect snapshots for unexpected *.py under component subdirs and root) and the CVE-2026-44827 None.py string. Legit diffusion repos ship code only as a root pipeline.py under intentional trust_remote_code use, so .py under unet/scheduler/etc. or a None.py in the HF cache is high-fidelity. Cross-checked Infosecurity Magazine and the GitLab advisory which confirm the None.py filename-construction bypass. Cross-checked against: • https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/hugging-face-diffusers-trust/ • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/diffusers/CVE-2026-44827/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Data scientist intentionally using trust_remote_code=True with an audited community pipeline that ships a root pipeline.py (should NOT hit component-subdir logic, but a custom repo may place helper .py under subfolders)
  • Internal ML platform team caching their own vetted custom diffusion pipelines to a shared HF_HOME
  • A model repo whose author legitimately named a scheduler/ subfolder that happens to contain a config-generation helper .py
  • Security researchers reproducing FaceHugger in a sandbox
  • Backup/restore or rsync of an existing HF cache re-writing .py files
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has_any ("/vetted-pipelines/","\\vetted-pipelines\\") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "trust_remote_code=True")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the FolderPath, FileName, SHA256 and InitiatingProcessCommandLine; open the file — a valid model never needs code under unet/scheduler/vae. Check FileOriginUrl / the from_pretrained repo id and whether trust_remote_code was actually intended. 2) Contain: isolate the host/CI runner, kill the python process, quarantine the cached snapshot directory, and revoke any credentials/tokens exposed to that process (registry keys, cloud creds, HF tokens). 3) Hunt: pivot on the repo id and SHA256 across all hosts, check for child processes/network egress from that python PID (UC2/UC3), and confirm diffusers>=0.38.0 is deployed everywhere loading models.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName endswith ".py"
| where FolderPath has "huggingface"
| where FileName =~ "None.py"
    or FolderPath has "diffusers_modules"
    or FolderPath has_any ("unet","scheduler","vae","text_encoder","safety_checker","feature_extractor","tokenizer")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName startswith "python"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileOriginUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFileName endswith ".py"
| where TargetFilePath has "huggingface"
| where TargetFileName =~ "None.py"
    or TargetFilePath has "diffusers_modules"
    or TargetFilePath has_any ("unet","scheduler","vae","text_encoder","safety_checker","feature_extractor","tokenizer")
| where ActingProcessName has "python"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Python interpreter spawning shell / LOLBin child after Diffusers model load (FaceHugger RCE) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the execution stage of the FaceHugger RCE: the malicious custom-pipeline code runs inside the Python interpreter during from_pretrained() and then spawns a command shell or download/network LOLBin (sh, bash, cmd, powershell, curl, wget, nc). A python parent launching an interactive shell or netcat is abnormal for a model-loading workload. Rationale: The article states custom-pipeline code executes in-process during from_pretrained(); the observable outcome is the python interpreter spawning an OS shell or network tool it would never legitimately need for model loading. Parent=python + child=shell/nc is the article-specific execution pivot rather than a generic template. Tiered as hunting because ML/CI code legitimately shells out. Cross-checked against: • https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/hugging-face-diffusers-trust/
ATT&CKT1059.006 T1059.004 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Jupyter/notebook cells using os.system or subprocess to run shell commands (git, ffmpeg, nvidia-smi)
  • CI/CD Python build scripts invoking bash/curl to fetch dependencies or artifacts
  • MLOps tooling shelling out to aws/gcloud CLIs from Python
  • Python-based installers calling powershell for environment setup on Windows
  • Data-prep pipelines calling wget/curl to download datasets
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("pip ","pip3 ","conda ","setup.py","ansible","nvidia-smi") or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("git ","ffmpeg","nvidia-smi","aws ","gcloud "))
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the parent python CommandLine and the child ProcessCommandLine — determine whether the python was running a legitimate script vs. a from_pretrained() model load, and whether the child performs recon (whoami/id), download (curl/wget) or a reverse shell (bash -i, nc -e). 2) Contain: kill the process chain, isolate the host/runner, and rotate any secrets reachable by that python context. 3) Hunt: correlate to UC1 (was a suspicious .py just written to the HF cache on this host?) and UC3 (outbound C2 from the same PID); sweep the fleet for the same repo id / SHA256 and for other python->shell chains in the surrounding window.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName startswith "python"
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh","pwsh.exe","curl","curl.exe","wget","nc","ncat")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName matches regex @"(?i)python[0-9.]*(\.exe)?$"
| where TargetProcessName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh","pwsh.exe","curl","curl.exe","wget","nc","ncat")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Outbound C2 from python process to non-Hugging Face public host (post-FaceHugger RCE) AICommand & Control Low
Anti-baseline hunt for a python process making outbound connections to public hosts that are not Hugging Face / package-registry / PyTorch infrastructure. After the crafted repo achieves code execution, the payload typically beacons or pulls a second stage; this surfaces python egress to unexpected external destinations. Pair with UC1/UC2 for confirmation. Rationale: The article frames a routine model load as an 'initial-access vector' granting extensive access, implying second-stage/C2 activity after execution. Since the only legitimate external egress for a diffusers load is HF/CDN/registry infrastructure, python connecting to any other public host is the article-relevant anomaly. Explicitly allowlists huggingface.co (the article's own domain) plus PyPI/PyTorch/GitHub to isolate the anomalous shape. sentinel_kql left empty: Sentinel's available network telemetry (ImNetworkSession/CommonSecurityLog) does not carry the initiating process image, so python-attributed egress cannot be expressed on this schema. Cross-checked against: • https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/hugging-face-diffusers-trust/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1059.006
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Python apps calling external APIs (OpenAI, weights hosting, wandb, HTTP inference endpoints) not on the allowlist
  • Model repos hosted on non-HF mirrors or S3/GCS buckets
  • Telemetry/crash-reporting or license-check callbacks from ML libraries
  • Data-fetching scripts hitting arbitrary dataset URLs
  • Package installs pulling from a private/self-hosted PyPI index
Suppression filter
| where not (RemoteUrl has_any ("openai.com","wandb.ai","amazonaws.com","googleapis.com","blob.core.windows.net"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: review the destination IP/domain reputation and the python InitiatingProcessCommandLine — is this a known API the app uses, or a rare/never-seen host? Check whether the same host wrote a suspicious HF cache .py (UC1) or spawned a shell (UC2) minutes earlier. 2) Contain: if the destination is unrecognized, block it at egress, isolate the host, and rotate exposed tokens/creds. 3) Hunt: sweep for other hosts beaconing to the same IP/domain, extend the window to find the triggering from_pretrained() repo id, and add confirmed-bad destinations to threat intel.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName startswith "python"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where not (RemoteUrl has_any ("huggingface.co","hf.co","hf-mirror.com","cdn-lfs","pytorch.org","pythonhosted.org","pypi.org","githubusercontent.com","github.com"))
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), Connections=count(), Ports=make_set(RemotePort, 15) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl
| order by FirstSeen desc

| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

    from datamodel=Email.All_Email

          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer

status: experimental
description: |

    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.

    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02

Coldcard Hardware Wallet Flaw Linked to $70 Million Bitcoin Theft in 41 Minutes

The Hacker News
2026-08-01 4 use cases 3 techniques 3 kill-chain phases detected

An attacker drained 1,196 Bitcoin addresses in 41 minutes on July 30, taking 1,082.65 BTC worth about $70.2 million at the time. Galaxy Research mapped the sweep and tied it to a firmware flaw in Coldcard, the Bitcoin-only hardware wallet made by Canadian firm Coinkite. A March 2021 firmware integration error routed seed generation to a deterministic software pseudorandom number generator (PRNG

Actions on Objectives
—
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Active Storage crafted image upload to libvips variant endpoints (CVE-2026-66066) · [LLM] Exposure hunt: hosts with vulnerable libvips / Rails Active Storage (CVE-2026-66066)

Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.

Active Storage crafted image upload to libvips variant endpoints (CVE-2026-66066) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts unauthenticated traffic to Rails Active Storage upload and variant/representation endpoints, the exploitation surface for CVE-2026-66066 (KindaRails2Shell) where a crafted image drives libvips into an arbitrary-file-read. Surfaces sources that both submit uploads and request server-side image processing so an analyst can triage the file-read primitive. Rationale: Uses the canonical Rails Active Storage route prefixes (/rails/active_storage/direct_uploads, /representations/, /blobs/, /disk/) — corroborated by Rapid7/Ethiack as the direct-upload + variant-processing surface. Technical PoC strings were withheld by the researchers, so this is a triage hunt on the exploit surface rather than a signature. Cross-checked against: • https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/etr-kindarails2shell-cve-2026-66066-critical-arbitrary-file-read-and-possible-remote-code-execution-in-ruby-on-rails/ • https://ethiack.com/info-hub/research/kindarails2shell-rails-rce-cve-2026-66066 • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/critical-rails-flaw-could-let.html
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate users uploading avatars/profile pictures and viewing generated thumbnails
  • Load/synthetic monitoring hitting upload endpoints
  • CDN or image-proxy warming Active Storage representations in bulk
  • Mobile app clients using direct_uploads at high volume
  • Security scanners (internal ASM/DAST) probing the same routes
Suppression filter
| where isnotempty(SrcIpAddr) and SrcIpAddr !in ("127.0.0.1", "::1")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the raw requests for the top source IPs — check whether they are unauthenticated, whether upload requests are immediately followed by representation/variant requests, and whether responses are anomalously sized (leaked file content). 2) Contain: if libvips <8.13 or the app is unpatched (Rails <7.2.3.2/8.0.5.1/8.1.3.1), block the source at the WAF/reverse-proxy and enable VIPS_BLOCK_UNTRUSTED. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host to UC 'Rails worker sensitive-file access' and 'Rails worker spawning shell/network child' to confirm file-read and RCE.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has "/rails/active_storage/"
| where Url has_any ("/representations/", "/blobs/", "/direct_uploads", "/disk/")
| summarize Requests = count(), Methods = make_set(HttpMethod, 10), Statuses = make_set(HttpStatusCode, 10), SampleUrls = make_set(Url, 10), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SrcIpAddr, HttpHostName
| order by LastSeen desc

Rails/Ruby worker reading secret_key_base and credential files post-upload (CVE-2026-66066) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the Rails application process (ruby/puma/unicorn/passenger) accessing sensitive secret and environment files — the credential-access step of CVE-2026-66066 where the libvips arbitrary-file-read is used to exfiltrate secret_key_base, master.key, credentials.yml.enc, .env and /proc/self/environ. High-fidelity because a running web worker should not be reading these at request time. Rationale: Ties the standard Rails secret paths named in the article (secret_key_base, master.key, database/cloud creds in the process environment) to the app-server process identity — a Rails worker reading /proc/self/environ or master.key at runtime is the direct fingerprint of the file-read primitive being abused. Cross-checked against: • https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/etr-kindarails2shell-cve-2026-66066-critical-arbitrary-file-read-and-possible-remote-code-execution-in-ruby-on-rails/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/critical-rails-flaw-could-let.html • https://socprime.com/blog/cve-2026-66066-critical-rails-flaw-exposes-server-files-via-image-uploads/
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1552
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Normal app boot reading config/master.key and credentials.yml.enc during initialization (baseline once per deploy/restart)
  • dotenv gems loading .env at startup
  • Config-management/CI tooling templating credential files
  • APM/observability agents enumerating process environment
  • Developer console (rails c) sessions on a jump host
Suppression filter
| where ActionType != "FileCreated" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "rails console" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "assets:precompile"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the access is at request-serving time (not process boot) and correlate the host/timestamp with UC1 Active Storage upload traffic within the same window. 2) Contain: treat secret_key_base, DB and Active Storage credentials as compromised — rotate them, rotate the Rails master key, and patch to Rails 7.2.3.2/8.0.5.1/8.1.3.1 with libvips ≥8.13. 3) Hunt: search for forged session cookies / anomalous authenticated sessions and pivot to UC3 for shell/network children of the worker.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ruby", "puma", "unicorn", "passenger", "bundle", "rails")
| where FileName in~ ("credentials.yml.enc", "master.key", "environ", ".env")
    or FolderPath has_any ("/config/credentials", "/proc/self/environ")
| where FolderPath !startswith "/tmp/" and FolderPath !has "/active_storage/"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessId, FileName, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("ruby", "puma", "unicorn", "passenger", "bundle", "rails")
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/config/credentials.yml.enc", "/config/master.key", "/config/credentials/", "/proc/self/environ")
    or TargetFileName =~ ".env"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessId, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Rails app worker spawning shell or network child (KindaRails2Shell RCE) AIInstallation High
Detects the Rails/Ruby application server (puma/unicorn/passenger/ruby) spawning an unexpected shell or network client (sh, bash, curl, wget, nc, python, ruby -e) — the RCE execution stage where a forged, secret_key_base-signed serialized payload drives insecure deserialization into command execution on the host. Rationale: A web application worker (puma/unicorn/passenger/ruby) is not expected to fork shells or curl/wget at runtime; pairing that specific parent set with shell/network children is the highest-fidelity signal of the deserialization-to-RCE endgame the article and Akamai describe. Cross-checked against: • https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/etr-kindarails2shell-cve-2026-66066-critical-arbitrary-file-read-and-possible-remote-code-execution-in-ruby-on-rails/ • https://ethiack.com/info-hub/research/kindarails2shell-rails-rce-cve-2026-66066
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1059
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Rails app legitimately shelling out to ImageMagick/ffmpeg/git via system() for background jobs
  • Sidekiq/Resque workers running rake tasks that invoke curl/bash
  • Health-check or entrypoint scripts (bash) launched by the app container
  • Deploy hooks calling shell from within the app process
  • Ruby scripts using backticks for legitimate ops tooling
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("convert", "identify", "vipsthumbnail", "ffmpeg", "/rake", "sidekiq", "healthcheck"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the child command line — reverse-shell one-liners, curl to unknown IPs, or writes to /tmp are strong TP indicators; benign image/rake tooling is FP. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the spawned process tree, and treat app secrets as compromised (rotate secret_key_base + all DB/cloud creds). 3) Hunt: pull outbound connections from the child, correlate back to the originating Active Storage upload (UC1) and credential-file reads (UC2), and search other Rails hosts for the same parent→child pattern.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ruby", "puma", "unicorn", "passenger", "rails", "bundle")
| where FileName in~ ("sh", "bash", "dash", "curl", "wget", "nc", "ncat", "python", "python3", "perl")
    or (FileName in~ ("ruby") and ProcessCommandLine has "-e ")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("ruby", "puma", "unicorn", "passenger", "rails", "bundle")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("/sh", "/bash", "/dash", "/curl", "/wget", "/nc", "/ncat", "/python", "/perl")
    or (ActingProcessName has "/ruby" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "-e ")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Exposure hunt: hosts with vulnerable libvips / Rails Active Storage (CVE-2026-66066) AIExploitation High
Surfaces internet-facing hosts still exposed to CVE-2026-66066 — libvips before 8.13 (which cannot disable the unfuzzed operations at all) or unpatched Rails Active Storage. Drives pre-exploitation prioritization since public PoCs are already circulating. Rationale: Directly keys on the article's named CVE (CVE-2026-66066) and the libvips 8.13 fix floor; scoping to internet-facing hosts turns the vuln feed into an actionable, prioritized exposure list ahead of the disclosed public PoCs. Cross-checked against: • https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/etr-kindarails2shell-cve-2026-66066-critical-arbitrary-file-read-and-possible-remote-code-execution-in-ruby-on-rails/ • https://www.linuxcompatible.org/story/rails-7232-8051-and-8131-active-storage-security-patch-targets-cve202666066
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Hosts that use ImageMagick (not libvips) as the Active Storage processor — not actually exploitable
  • Apps that do not accept untrusted image uploads (internal-only) — lower real risk
  • TVM version-string mismatch flagging a backported/distro-patched libvips as vulnerable
  • Rails 6.x using Active Storage defaults (not affected) still flagged by generic version match
  • Decommissioned/quarantined hosts still in inventory
Response runbook
1) Triage: for each flagged host confirm it uses the vips processor and accepts untrusted uploads (else de-prioritize), and check internet exposure. 2) Contain: patch Active Storage to 7.2.3.2/8.0.5.1/8.1.3.1, upgrade libvips to ≥8.13, and set VIPS_BLOCK_UNTRUSTED / Vips.block_untrusted(true); apply WAF virtual patch where immediate upgrade isn't possible. 3) Hunt: retro-scan UC1/UC2/UC3 telemetry on every exposed host for prior exploitation before the patch window.

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01

description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"

    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-66066")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-66066")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Hackers Poison Adform Script to Swap Crypto Wallet Addresses Across Customer Sites

The Hacker News
2026-08-01 12 use cases 5 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Attackers modified a JavaScript file served by advertising technology company Adform, turning it into a browser-side tool that rewrites cryptocurrency wallet addresses. Adform detected the incident on July 27, 2026, removed the malicious code, notified affected clients, and reported it to authorities. Anyone who visited a site carrying the affected script on July 27 and copied a Bitcoin,

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Adform poisoned script load correlated with C2 beacon (supply-chain confirmation) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Hackers Poison Adform Script to Swap Crypto Wallet Addresses Across Customer Sit
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Adform crypto-swap payload C2 beacon to 84.32.102.230:7744 · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
Adform crypto-swap payload C2 beacon to 84.32.102.230:7744 AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts any host beaconing to the attacker-controlled server 84.32.102.230 (port 7744) used by the trojanized Adform trackpoint-async.js crypto-address-swapper. The poisoned script issues an HTTP request to this IP on page load carrying the visitor's hostname and path, so any egress to this dedicated malicious IP indicates a browser that rendered the compromised script. Rationale: 84.32.102.230:7744 is the hard IOC — a dedicated attacker VPS confirmed by both Beaumont/DoublePulsar and BleepingComputer as the endpoint the poisoned Adform script beacons to with visitor hostname/path. A single-IP match on a raw-IP, non-standard-port destination is inherently high-fidelity; unusual port 7744 further separates it from CDN noise. Cross-checked against: • https://doublepulsar.com/adform-compromised-to-serve-crypto-stealer-via-supply-chain-attack-2f1ec024f33e • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/online-ad-firm-adforms-script-compromised-to-steal-cryptocurrency/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1041 T1565.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A malware analyst or automated sandbox detonating the captured trackpoint-async.js sample from a corporate range
  • Threat-intel enrichment/scanning tooling (e.g. a TIP connector) actively probing the IOC IP
  • Security researcher curling/replaying the C2 during investigation
  • Post-takedown reassignment of the VPS IP 84.32.102.230 to an unrelated benign hosting tenant
  • IR team validating the IOC from a jump box
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe","iexplore.exe")  // real victims beacon from the browser render context; drops analyst/curl/python detonation noise
Response runbook
1) Triage: On each hit, pull InitiatingProcessFileName/ComputerName — a browser (chrome/msedge/firefox) reaching this IP confirms a victim; identify the last-loaded page URL to find which Adform-carrying site exposed them. 2) Contain: Block 84.32.102.230 at egress/firewall/proxy, force-clear browser cache on affected hosts (the poisoned file may still be cached), and warn users to re-verify any crypto wallet address before sending. 3) Hunt: Pivot to all hosts that loaded s2.adform.net/trackpoint-async.js in the window, and review any outbound cryptocurrency transactions made from affected endpoints on/after July 27 2026 for altered destination wallets.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "84.32.102.230"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP == "84.32.102.230"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestURL, ApplicationProtocol, DeviceAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Adform Supply-Chain Crypto-Swap C2 Beacon (84.32.102.230)

Adform poisoned script load correlated with C2 beacon (supply-chain confirmation) AIDelivery High
Confirms the Adform supply-chain vector by correlating, per host, a load of s2.adform.net/trackpoint-async.js with an outbound connection to the crypto-swap C2 at 84.32.102.230. This ties the malicious egress specifically to the trojanized third-party ad script rather than any coincidental hit on the IP, and maps the initial-access supply-chain surface. Rationale: Combines the two corroborated article facts — the poisoned resource path (s2.adform.net/.../trackpoint-async.js) and the C2 IP (84.32.102.230) — into a same-host correlation, which is near-zero FP and explicitly attributes the egress to the Adform supply-chain vector. Datadog/CloudWatch/Sigma omitted because this is a two-event cross-source correlation those single-query surfaces can't express. Cross-checked against: • https://doublepulsar.com/adform-compromised-to-serve-crypto-stealer-via-supply-chain-attack-2f1ec024f33e • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/online-ad-firm-adforms-script-compromised-to-steal-cryptocurrency/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1185 T1071.001
Data sourcesWeb Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Proxy-log variant: many users behind one NAT/egress SourceIP can falsely correlate an Adform load by user A with a beacon by unrelated process B — use the EDR (DeviceId) variant where per-host attribution is exact
  • Malware analyst host that both loaded the sample page and beaconed during investigation
  • Post-takedown reassignment of 84.32.102.230 to a benign service still coincident with legitimate Adform loads
  • A synthetic monitoring/RUM agent that loads Adform-carrying pages and is separately allowed to the IOC IP
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")  // constrain to browser-render context so the load and beacon share the true victim process lineage
Response runbook
1) Triage: Confirm the same DeviceId shows both the trackpoint-async.js load and the 84.32.102.230 beacon within the same browsing session; capture the AdformUrl and referring page. 2) Contain: Block 84.32.102.230 at egress, clear/invalidate the cached Adform script fleet-wide (cache-busting or forced cache clear), and notify finance/treasury and any users who transacted crypto to re-verify destination addresses. 3) Hunt: Enumerate every internal host that loaded s2.adform.net/trackpoint-async.js since ~July 20 2026 (Beaumont observed activity for a week before the July 27 fix) and review outbound crypto payments from those hosts for wallet substitution.
let LookbackDays = 30d;
let AdformLoads = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where RemoteUrl has "s2.adform.net" and RemoteUrl has "trackpoint-async.js"
    | project AdformTime = Timestamp, DeviceId, AdformUrl = RemoteUrl, LoadProc = InitiatingProcessFileName;
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where RemoteIP == "84.32.102.230"
| project BeaconTime = Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| join kind=inner AdformLoads on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, AdformUrl, AdformTime, BeaconTime, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by BeaconTime desc
let LookbackDays = 30d;
let AdformLoads = CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where RequestURL has "s2.adform.net" and RequestURL has "trackpoint-async.js"
    | project AdformTime = TimeGenerated, SourceIP, AdformUrl = RequestURL;
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where DestinationIP == "84.32.102.230"
| project BeaconTime = TimeGenerated, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationIP, DestinationPort
| join kind=inner AdformLoads on SourceIP
| project SourceIP, SourceUserName, AdformUrl, AdformTime, BeaconTime, DestinationIP, DestinationPort
| order by BeaconTime desc
