Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Device code phishing token redemption via Microsoft Authentication Broker sign-in · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] ARToken post-token abuse: inbox rules & SharePoint exfil from device-code sign-in IP · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Device code phishing token redemption via Microsoft Authentication Broker sign-in AIExploitation Medium
Hunts successful Entra sign-ins through the Microsoft Authentication Broker app (AppId 29d9ed98-a469-4536-ade2-f981bc1d605e) against Device Registration Service / Microsoft Graph — the redemption footprint of an OAuth device authorization grant token captured by device code phishing kits (Storm-2372, EvilTokens/ARToken, DEBULL). This is the only server-side artifact of a device code phish since the victim interacts with legitimate Microsoft URLs. Rationale: Pivots on the concrete Microsoft Authentication Broker AppId (29d9ed98-a469-4536-ade2-f981bc1d605e) + Device Registration Service resource, the redemption footprint documented across Storm-2372 (Microsoft) and DEBULL (ZeroBEC) — the only reliable server-side artifact given the article's point that the flow transits legitimate Microsoft URLs. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/02/13/storm-2372-conducts-device-code-phishing-campaign/ • https://zerobec.com/blog/debull-storm-2372-microsoft-device-code-phishing-graphspy • https://www.wiz.io/blog/recent-oauth-attacks-detection-strategies
ATT&CKT1528 T1566.002
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Intune/Autopilot device enrollment which also transacts through the Microsoft Authentication Broker
  • Developers authenticating CLI tools or WAM broker on new corporate laptops
  • Windows Hello for Business provisioning against Device Registration Service
  • BYOD workplace-join of a personal device by a genuine employee
  • Conditional Access-driven re-registration after a device reset
Suppression filter
// Suppress users who routinely redeem via the broker (baseline) — leftanti against 30d history
let Baseline = SigninLogs | where TimeGenerated between (ago(30d) .. ago(2d)) | where AppId == "29d9ed98-a469-4536-ade2-f981bc1d605e" | summarize by UserPrincipalName; // join kind=leftanti on UserPrincipalName to surface first-time redeemers only
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: For each hit pull the IPAddress/Location and compare against the user's normal interactive sign-in geo/ASN in SigninLogs; a broker sign-in from an IP the user never uses interactively is high suspicion. 2) CONTAIN: If unrecognized, revoke the user's refresh tokens (Revoke-MgUserSignInSession), disable/quarantine any device object registered in the same window, and force re-auth. 3) HUNT: Check AuditLogs for a 'Register device'/'Add device' event by the same user (PRT persistence) and OfficeActivity for inbox-rule or SharePoint/OneDrive bulk download from the broker IP.
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ErrorCode == 0
| where ApplicationId == "29d9ed98-a469-4536-ade2-f981bc1d605e" or AppDisplayName == "Microsoft Authentication Broker"
| where ResourceDisplayName in ("Device Registration Service","Microsoft Graph")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), SignIns=count(), IPs=make_set(IPAddress,10), Countries=make_set(Country,10) by AccountUpn, AppDisplayName, ResourceDisplayName, ClientAppUsed
| order by FirstSeen desc
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == 0
| where AppId == "29d9ed98-a469-4536-ade2-f981bc1d605e" or AppDisplayName == "Microsoft Authentication Broker"
| where ResourceDisplayName in ("Device Registration Service","Microsoft Graph")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), SignIns=count(), IPs=make_set(IPAddress,10), Locations=make_set(Location,10) by UserPrincipalName, AppDisplayName, ResourceDisplayName, ClientAppUsed
| order by FirstSeen desc

CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

ARToken post-token abuse: inbox rules & SharePoint exfil from device-code sign-in IP AIActions on Objectives Medium
Ties a Microsoft Authentication Broker device-code sign-in to subsequent mailbox rule creation or bulk SharePoint/OneDrive downloads from the SAME source IP — the BEC-automation and SharePoint-exfiltration features Cisco Talos documents in the ARToken EvilTokens panel. Scoping to the broker sign-in IP separates attacker token use from the legitimate user's activity. Rationale: Anchors OfficeActivity/CloudAppEvents inbox-rule and SharePoint/OneDrive download operations to the same source IP that performed the Microsoft Authentication Broker device-code sign-in — matching ARToken's advertised BEC automation + SharePoint exfiltration feature set (Talos), and eliminating the legitimate user's own activity from the same account. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/artoken-inside-an-eviltokens-affiliate-panel-targeting-microsoft-365/ • https://blog.knowbe4.com/warning-artoken-phishing-kit-automates-bec-attacksartoken-phishing-kit-automates-bec-attacks • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/artoken-phaas-exposes-eviltokens-microsoft-365-phishing-toolkit/
ATT&CKT1114.003 T1530 T1567.002
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User legitimately working from home/VPN whose interactive and broker sign-ins share the same IP and who creates a genuine rule
  • Bulk OneDrive sync of a large document library on a newly enrolled device
  • Automated backup/eDiscovery tooling authenticating via broker and downloading files
  • Admin-configured transport/inbox rules pushed during onboarding
  • Legitimate SharePoint site migration from the same egress IP
Suppression filter
// Drop matches where the broker IP is also the user's habitual interactive IP (not attacker infra)
// join kind=leftanti against SigninLogs interactive sign-ins (IsInteractive==true) on UserId+ClientIP before alerting
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Review the make_set of inbox rules and downloaded file names; forwarding-to-external or hide-in-RSS rules plus >50 unique files is high confidence. 2) CONTAIN: Revoke tokens/PRTs, delete malicious inbox rules, disable external forwarding, and block the source IP at CA/named-locations; notify the mailbox owner of potential BEC. 3) HUNT: Enumerate all mailboxes/sites touched from the same ClientIP, check for outbound BEC replies in the thread, and correlate with UC1/UC2 hits for the same principal.
let brokerIPs = AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ErrorCode == 0
| where ApplicationId == "29d9ed98-a469-4536-ade2-f981bc1d605e" or AppDisplayName == "Microsoft Authentication Broker"
| summarize by AccountObjectId, IPAddress;
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("New-InboxRule","Set-InboxRule","FileDownloaded","FileSyncDownloadedFull")
| join kind=inner brokerIPs on AccountObjectId, IPAddress
| summarize Ops=count(), Actions=make_set(ActionType,10), Objects=make_set(ObjectName,10), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp) by AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, Application, IPAddress
| order by Ops desc
let brokerIPs = SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == 0
| where AppId == "29d9ed98-a469-4536-ade2-f981bc1d605e" or AppDisplayName == "Microsoft Authentication Broker"
| summarize by UserId=UserPrincipalName, ClientIP=IPAddress;
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Operation in ("New-InboxRule","Set-InboxRule","FileDownloaded","FileSyncDownloadedFull")
| join kind=inner brokerIPs on UserId, ClientIP
| summarize Ops=count(), Operations=make_set(Operation,10), Files=make_set(SourceFileName,20), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated) by UserId, OfficeWorkload, ClientIP
| order by Ops desc

DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent

| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```

    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes

                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo

Chinese Hacker Commands DeepSeek via Telegram to Launch Autonomous Attacks

The Hacker News
2026-07-31 10 use cases 3 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Palo Alto Networks' Unit 42 says a Chinese-speaking threat actor used DeepSeek through the open-source Hermes Agent framework to launch attacks autonomously. After an initial Telegram instruction, the agent found internet-facing systems and selected public exploits. The researchers recovered no further operator input in the session. The operator, tracked through the aliases knaithe and KnYuan,

Hermes/DeepSeek autonomous AI agent artifact: python3 -m http.server 8888 from /home/worker AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the opsec-failure artifact that exposed this campaign: the Hermes Agent (DeepSeek-driven, 'Yolo' unattended mode) launched a Python stdlib file server on port 8888 out of /home/worker, exposing exploit scripts, API keys and session logs. This surfaces the same autonomous-agent tooling running on your own Linux fleet or on a compromised host being used as a staging box. Rationale: Uses the exact opsec artifact Unit 42 named — 'Hermes Agent exposed the operation by starting python3 -m http.server 8888 from /home/worker'. The http.server module + fixed port 8888 combination is the high-fidelity anchor; the /home/worker CWD / 'worker' account is projected as an enrichment flag. Cross-checked Unit 42 and BleepingComputer. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/autonomous-ai-cyber-attack-campaign/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hacker-uses-deepseek-ai-to-autonomously-attack-vulnerable-servers/
ATT&CKT1059.006 T1071.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Data scientist / developer running 'python -m http.server 8888' to quickly share files on a lab host
  • CI runner or container serving build artifacts over the stdlib http server on 8888
  • Internal documentation preview served with http.server on the conventional 8888 port
  • Ad-hoc troubleshooting of a Jupyter-adjacent workflow where 8888 is the habitual port
Suppression filter
| where not (AccountName in~ ("jenkins","gitlab-runner","builder") and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("bash","sh") and ProcessCommandLine has "/build/")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full process tree and shell history around the http.server PID — confirm the CWD and enumerate sibling processes (exploit scripts, curl/wget to FOFA/GitHub, other python agents). Check whether the parent is an interactive shell (benign dev) vs an unattended agent/cron. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the listener, and rotate any API keys/tokens present under the serving directory (Hermes exposed model API keys). 3) Hunt: on the same host look for outbound to FOFA/GitHub raw-content, downloaded public exploit files, and marimo/n8n/langflow scanning cmdlines; sweep the fleet for other :8888 http.server listeners.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("python","python3")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "http.server" and ProcessCommandLine has "8888"
| extend HermesHomeDir = (ProcessCommandLine has "/home/worker" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "/home/worker" or AccountName =~ "worker")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, HermesHomeDir
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("python","python3")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "http.server" and TargetProcessCommandLine has "8888"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcess = ActingProcessName, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Marimo CVE-2026-39987 pre-auth RCE: marimo notebook process spawning a shell AIExploitation High
Hunts successful exploitation of the Marimo unauthenticated /terminal/ws WebSocket flaw, where an attacker obtains a root PTY shell. Detection fires when the marimo notebook server process spawns an interactive shell or recon/download binary — the direct post-RCE landing that the agent used to run commands on 11 Marimo instances. Rationale: Corroborated via GitHub advisory GHSA-2679-6mx9-h9xc / Resecurity: the /terminal/ws endpoint skips validate_auth() and hands back a root PTY, so a marimo (python) parent spawning sh/bash/curl is the unambiguous RCE landing. Parent keyed on 'marimo' in cmdline/path; alternative web-log angle is a WebSocket upgrade to /terminal/ws. Datadog left empty — auditd parent-process correlation isn't expressible with the documented Datadog linux.auditd fields. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-2679-6mx9-h9xc • https://www.resecurity.com/blog/article/marimo-pre-auth-rce-via-unauthenticated-websocket-terminal-cve-2026-39987 • https://thehackernews.com/2026/04/marimo-rce-flaw-cve-2026-39987.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate notebook code cells that shell out (subprocess/os.system) to run tooling as part of a data pipeline
  • Marimo admin running a terminal deliberately for maintenance
  • Container entrypoint scripts where marimo is the PID 1 wrapper spawning shell helpers on startup
  • CI job that launches marimo and immediately shells to install dependencies
Suppression filter
| where not (ChildProcess in~ ("python","python3") and ChildCmd has "pip install")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the child shell's command line and downstream activity (whoami/id showing root, curl/wget of second-stage payloads). Correlate with a web request to /terminal/ws around the same timestamp and check the source IP against the >460-target scanning infrastructure. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the marimo process and shell, and confirm Marimo is upgraded to >=0.23.0 (fixed build). 3) Hunt: pull all commands run via the PTY, look for persistence (cron, systemd, SSH keys), and sweep for other internet-exposed marimo/notebook interfaces still on vulnerable versions.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "marimo" or InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "marimo" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "marimo"
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","curl","wget","id","whoami","python","python3")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ChildProcess = FileName, ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "marimo" or ActingProcessName =~ "marimo"
| where TargetProcessName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","curl","wget","id","whoami","python","python3")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcess = ActingProcessName, ParentCmd = ActingProcessCommandLine, ChildProcess = TargetProcessName, ChildCmd = TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

NetScaler CVE-2026-3055 SAML IdP memory overread: high-volume /saml/login scraping AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts exploitation of the Citrix NetScaler SAML IdP memory-overread flaw used to exfiltrate data from three organizations. A single source repeatedly hits the SAML IdP /saml/login endpoint to leak leftover request memory (session tokens/data) — abnormal versus real users who authenticate once. Applies to customer-managed NetScaler ADC/Gateway configured as a SAML IdP. Rationale: Anchored on the corroborated exploitation primitive: Horizon3/watchTowr/Fortinet confirm CVE-2026-3055 is triggered by repeated requests to the SAML IdP '/saml/login' endpoint (NSC_TASS) to over-read appliance memory, and the article ties this to data exfil from three orgs. A single source hammering /saml/login 100+ times per 10m is the differentiator from legitimate single-shot SAML logins. Defender/Falcon/Datadog left empty — NetScaler appliance web telemetry lands in Sentinel CEF and web-proxy datamodels, not endpoint EDR; Sigma skipped because this is a volumetric/threshold detection. Cross-checked against: • https://horizon3.ai/attack-research/vulnerabilities/cve-2026-3055/ • https://watchtowr.com/resources/rapid-reaction-to-cve-2026-3055/ • https://threat-modeling.com/citrix-netscaler-saml-idp-cve-2026-3055/
ATT&CKT1190 T1552.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A busy legitimate SAML IdP fronting many apps where a NAT/egress gateway concentrates hundreds of real logins behind one SourceIP
  • Uptime/synthetic monitoring repeatedly probing the /saml/login health path
  • Load-testing or SSO integration testing hammering the IdP endpoint
  • A misconfigured SP retry loop re-requesting /saml/login
Suppression filter
| where DistinctUA <= 2 and SourceIP !in ("<corporate_nat_egress_ip>")
Response runbook
1) Triage: profile the top SourceIP — is it a corporate NAT egress (many real users) or a single external/hosting-provider IP with one user-agent and no successful auth follow-through? Inspect response sizes/status for the over-read pattern. 2) Contain: block the source at the NetScaler/WAF, and verify the appliance is on the fixed build (14.1-66.59 / 13.1-62.23 or later); if unpatched and configured as SAML IdP, treat leaked session material as compromised and rotate. 3) Hunt: correlate the SourceIP against inbound access to Langflow/n8n/marimo scanning, and review authenticated sessions from tokens that may have been leaked from appliance memory.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DeviceVendor has "Citrix" or DeviceProduct has_any ("NetScaler","ADC")
| where RequestURL has "/saml/login"
| summarize Requests = count(), DistinctUA = dcount(RequestClientApplication), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), SampleURLs = make_set(RequestURL, 5) by SourceIP, DestinationHostName, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where Requests > 100    // 100+ /saml/login hits from one source in 10m = memory scraping, not a real login
| order by Requests desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",

         by Processes.dest, Processes.user

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Network Anomaly Detection in KATA

Securelist (Kaspersky)
2026-07-31 6 use cases 4 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

An analysis of how Network Anomaly Detection (NAD) rules work within Kaspersky Anti Targeted Attack, using Kerberoasting and DNS tunneling attacks as examples.

ATT&CKT1021.001 T1190 T1558 T1558.003

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] DNS tunneling: host issuing many long unique subdomain queries under one parent domain · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains · DNS tunneling / TXT-heavy domain queries
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Kerberoasting: single account/host requesting TGS tickets for many unique non-system SPNs
Kerberoasting: single account/host requesting TGS tickets for many unique non-system SPNs AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the exact anomaly the KATA NAD 'Signs of a Kerberoasting attack' rule targets: one client account (cname) from one source IP receiving successful Kerberos TGS responses for N or more distinct service (non-machine) SPNs inside a short window. System/computer-account SPNs are excluded because they carry uncrackable auto-generated passwords, mirroring the article's excl logic. Fan-out volume, not encryption type, is the signal. Rationale: Anchors on the article's exact NAD logic — KRB_TGS_REP fan-out (dcount of non-'$' ServiceName per requesting cname/source IP) with system SPNs excluded and a count_spns threshold, rather than RC4 signature. MITRE DET0157 independently describes the same 'one account, many distinct SPNs, short window' pattern. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/detectionstrategies/DET0157/ • https://securelist.com/tr/network-anomaly-detection-in-kata/120892/
ATT&CKT1558.003
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Vulnerability scanners (Tenable/Qualys/BloodHound collectors) enumerating SPNs across the domain
  • SCCM/MECM or monitoring service accounts that legitimately touch many services at startup
  • A privileged admin workstation opening many Kerberos-authenticated apps (SQL, CIFS, HTTP) in a burst after logon
  • Backup/inventory tooling that iterates service accounts
  • Login storms after a DC reboot causing batched ticket requests
Suppression filter
| where TargetUserName !in~ ("svc-scanner","svc-bloodhound","svc-sccm") and IpAddress !in ("10.0.0.0/8-scanner-subnet")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pivot on TargetUserName + IpAddress; resolve the source host and confirm whether the account/host normally requests these SPNs. Check if requests came from a workstation vs a server and whether the targeted accounts are high-value (SQL/admin service accounts). 2) Contain: if unsanctioned, disable/force-reset the requesting account and any targeted service-account passwords (assume offline crack in progress), and isolate the source host. 3) Hunt: search for the same source IP performing LDAP SPN enumeration prior to the burst, subsequent logons using the targeted service accounts, and Rubeus/Impacket GetUserSPNs command-line artifacts on the source host.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where EventID == 4769
| where Status == "0x0"                       // successful TGS-REP only (article: KRB_TGS_REP)
| where ServiceName !endswith "$"             // exclude machine/computer-account SPNs (auto-generated strong passwords)
| where ServiceName !in~ ("krbtgt")
| where TargetUserName !endswith "$" and TargetUserName !in~ ("","-")
| summarize UniqueSPNs = dcount(ServiceName), TargetedSPNs = make_set(ServiceName, 25), TGSRequests = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
    by TargetUserName, IpAddress, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where UniqueSPNs >= 10           // count_spns threshold: single account pulling >=10 distinct service SPNs in 10m
| order by UniqueSPNs desc
source:windows.security @EventID:4769 -@TargetUserName:*$
ENDPOINT
`wineventlog_security` EventCode=4769 Service_Name!="*$" Service_Name!="krbtgt" Account_Name!="*$" Failure_Code="0x0"
| eval win=bin(_time, span=10m)
| stats dc(Service_Name) AS unique_spns values(Service_Name) AS targeted_spns count AS tgs_requests min(_time) AS firstTime max(_time) AS lastTime by Account_Name, Client_Address, win
| where unique_spns >= 10
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - unique_spns
DNS tunneling: host issuing many long unique subdomain queries under one parent domain AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the KATA 'Data tunneling in DNS traffic' anomaly: a single host emitting a high volume of unique, abnormally long subdomain labels under one parent zone (encoded data smuggled in the QNAME). Behaviour-based — thresholds on unique-subdomain count and label length rather than a static domain IOC — so it catches the article's example (e.g. crust.testinglab.ru-style beacons) and unknown tunnels alike. Rationale: Anchors on the article's KATA rule shape — per-source high volume of unique subdomains under a single parent zone, with long QNAMEs carrying encoded data — instead of the disposable lab IOC (testinglab.ru / crust.testinglab.ru is a Kaspersky test zone, not shipped as an IOC). MITRE DET0400 corroborates the long-label (>30 char) + abnormal query-volume-to-single-domain signals; thresholds set at 40-char avg / 50 unique labels. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/detectionstrategies/DET0400/ • https://securelist.com/tr/network-anomaly-detection-in-kata/120892/
ATT&CKT1071.004 T1048.003
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • CDN / anti-bot providers (Akamai, Cloudflare, CDN edge tokens) that embed long hashed labels in FQDNs
  • Antivirus/EDR cloud-reputation lookups that hash file/URL data into subdomains (e.g. McAfee, Sophos, Trend)
  • Telemetry/analytics SDKs beaconing device IDs as subdomain labels
  • Email security gateways doing SPF/DKIM/DMARC and RBL lookups in bulk
  • Legitimate DNS-based licensing or software-update check-ins with encoded tokens
Suppression filter
| where Parent !endswith "akamaiedge.net" and Parent !endswith "cloudflare.com" and Parent !endswith "trafficmanager.net" and Parent !endswith "amazonaws.com"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the parent zone and the initiating process/host; check domain age/registration and whether the zone is a known CDN/security vendor. Inspect sample QNAMEs for base32/base64/hex encoding and consistent length. 2) Contain: if the zone is unrecognised, sinkhole/block it at the resolver and isolate the source host; capture the process making the queries. 3) Hunt: pivot to other hosts querying the same parent zone, correlate to a non-browser/non-system parent process (powershell/rundll32/python) initiating the DNS, and look for matching TXT/NULL/CNAME record types indicative of a tunnel utility (iodine, dnscat2).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1h)
| where isnotempty(RemoteUrl)
| extend Labels = split(RemoteUrl, ".")
| where array_length(Labels) >= 3
| extend Parent = strcat(tostring(Labels[array_length(Labels)-2]), ".", tostring(Labels[array_length(Labels)-1]))
| where Parent !endswith "in-addr.arpa"
| summarize UniqueFqdns = dcount(RemoteUrl), AvgLen = avg(strlen(RemoteUrl)), MaxLen = max(strlen(RemoteUrl)), Conns = count(), Sample = make_set(RemoteUrl, 10)
    by DeviceName, Parent, bin(Timestamp, 10m)
| where UniqueFqdns >= 50 and AvgLen >= 40    // 50 distinct long labels under one zone in 10m = tunneling shape
| order by UniqueFqdns desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where isnotempty(Name)
| where Name !endswith ".in-addr.arpa" and Name !endswith ".arpa"
| extend Labels = split(Name, ".")
| where array_length(Labels) >= 3
| extend Parent = strcat(tostring(Labels[array_length(Labels)-2]), ".", tostring(Labels[array_length(Labels)-1]))
| extend TopLabelLen = strlen(tostring(Labels[0]))
| summarize UniqueSubdomains = dcount(Name), QueryCount = count(), AvgLen = avg(strlen(Name)), MaxTopLabel = max(TopLabelLen), Sample = make_set(Name, 10)
    by ClientIP, Parent, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where UniqueSubdomains >= 50 and AvgLen >= 40   // MITRE DET0400: many long unique labels to one zone
| order by UniqueSubdomains desc
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/.{40,}/
| regex("(?<parent>[a-z0-9-]+\.[a-z]+)$", field=DomainName)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, parent], function=[count(field=DomainName, distinct=true, as=unique_long_subdomains), count(as=total_queries)])
| unique_long_subdomains >= 50
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count AS query_count, dc(DNS.query) AS unique_subdomains, values(DNS.query) AS sample_queries FROM datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS WHERE nodename=DNS DNS.message_type="QUERY" BY DNS.src, DNS.query, _time span=10m
| eval parent=replace(DNS.query, "^.*?\.([^.]+\.[^.]+)$", "\1"), qlen=len(DNS.query)
| stats sum(query_count) AS total_queries, dc(DNS.query) AS unique_subdomains, avg(qlen) AS avg_len, max(qlen) AS max_len, values(sample_queries) AS sample_queries BY DNS.src, parent
| where unique_subdomains >= 50 AND avg_len >= 40
| sort - unique_subdomains
| tstats summariesonly=false count AS query_count, dc(DNS.query) AS unique_subdomains, values(DNS.query) AS sample_queries FROM datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS WHERE nodename=DNS DNS.message_type="QUERY" BY DNS.src, DNS.query, _time span=10m
| eval parent=replace(DNS.query, "^.*?\.([^.]+\.[^.]+)$", "\1"), qlen=len(DNS.query)
| stats sum(query_count) AS total_queries, dc(DNS.query) AS unique_subdomains, avg(qlen) AS avg_len, max(qlen) AS max_len, values(sample_queries) AS sample_queries BY DNS.src, parent
| where unique_subdomains >= 50 AND avg_len >= 40
| sort - unique_subdomains
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High
Outbound traffic to attacker infrastructure named in the article.
ATT&CKT1071
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web Network_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("") or RemoteUrl has_any ("testinglab.ru", "crust.testinglab.ru")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
let BadIPs     = dynamic([""]);
let BadDomains = dynamic(["testinglab.ru", "crust.testinglab.ru"]);
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstIpAddr in (BadIPs)
   or Url has_any (BadDomains)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, NetworkProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

DNS tunneling / TXT-heavy domain queries Command & Control Medium
Long subdomain labels + frequent queries to a single 2LD = DNS C2/exfil.
ATT&CKT1071.004 T1048.003
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemotePort == 53 and isnotempty(RemoteUrl)
| extend qlen = strlen(RemoteUrl)
| where qlen > 50
| extend SecondLevelDomain = extract(@"([\w-]+\.[a-zA-Z]{2,})$", 1, RemoteUrl)
| summarize qcount = count(), uniqueSubs = dcount(RemoteUrl), maxLabel = max(qlen)
    by DeviceName, SecondLevelDomain
| where qcount > 100 and uniqueSubs > 20
| order by qcount desc
// ASIM ImDnsActivity normalises Windows DNS, Sysmon EID 22, Linux dnsmasq, etc.
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where DnsQueryTypeName == "TXT"
| summarize Queries = count(), DistinctNames = dcount(DnsQuery)
            by SrcIpAddr, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| where Queries > 200    // tune to TXT-query baseline for environment
| order by Queries desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS
    where DNS.message_type="QUERY"
    by DNS.src, DNS.query
| `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)`
| eval qlen=len(query)
| where qlen > 50
| rex field=query "(?<second_level_domain>[\w-]+\.[\w-]+)$"
| stats sum(count) AS qcount, dc(query) AS unique_subs, max(qlen) AS max_label
    by src, second_level_domain
| where qcount > 100 AND unique_subs > 20
| sort - qcount
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS
    where DNS.message_type="QUERY"
    by DNS.src, DNS.query
| `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)`
| eval qlen=len(query)
| where qlen > 50
| rex field=query "(?<second_level_domain>[\w-]+\.[\w-]+)$"
| stats sum(count) AS qcount, dc(query) AS unique_subs, max(qlen) AS max_label
    by src, second_level_domain
| where qcount > 100 AND unique_subs > 20
| sort - qcount

schtasks.exe /create or Microsoft-Windows-TaskScheduler EventID 4698 with LOLBin actions.
ATT&CKT1053.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName =~ "schtasks.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "/create"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("powershell","cmd.exe","rundll32","-enc","FromBase64","\Users\Public","\AppData\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\schtasks.exe"
| where CommandLine has "/create"
| where CommandLine has_any ("powershell","cmd.exe","rundll32","-enc","FromBase64",
                              "\Users\Public", "\AppData\")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName, NewProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Scheduled Task Creation with Suspicious Image / Encoded Args
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0d
status: experimental
description: |
    schtasks.exe /create with payload-shaped action — points at
    powershell, cmd, rundll32, encoded-base64, or user-writable paths.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1053/005/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1053.005
    - attack.persistence
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_schtasks:
        Image|endswith: '\schtasks.exe'
        CommandLine|contains: '/create'
    selection_payload:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'powershell'
            - 'cmd.exe'
            - 'rundll32'
            - '-enc'
            - 'FromBase64'
            - '\Users\Public'
            - '\AppData\'
    condition: selection_schtasks and selection_payload
falsepositives:
    - GPO-driven scheduled tasks, MDT/SCCM imaging
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name="schtasks.exe" AND Processes.process="*/create*"

XCSSET v40 CDP hijack: Google Chrome launched with remote-debugging-port AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the XCSSET v40 Chrome-hijacking module activating the Chrome DevTools Protocol by relaunching the legitimate Google Chrome binary with --remote-debugging-port (and, post-Chrome-136, a non-default --user-data-dir) so the dropped chrome_remote binary can attach to the browser engine. Article-specific because it targets the exact CDP-enablement command line the wrapper uses on the real Chrome binary, not headless automation. Rationale: Uses the article's exact CDP-enablement behaviour (legitimate 'Google Chrome' binary + --remote-debugging-port, with --user-data-dir surfaced because Chrome 136+ ignores the switch on the default profile). Cross-checked against MITRE S0658 and vendor write-ups confirming the CDP module. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0658/ • https://www.securityweek.com/new-xcsset-macos-malware-variant-hijacks-cryptocurrency-transactions/ • https://thehackernews.com/2025/09/new-macos-xcsset-variant-targets.html
ATT&CKT1185 T1539 T1554
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developers running Selenium/Puppeteer/Playwright test suites that launch Chrome with a debugging port
  • chromedriver-driven CI/automation on developer laptops
  • Manual QA using `--remote-debugging-port` for front-end debugging
  • VS Code / JS debugger 'attach to Chrome' launch configs
  • Lighthouse / performance-profiling tooling launching Chrome with CDP
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chromedriver","node","python","python3","Code Helper") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "puppeteer" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "selenium"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the launching parent — automation binaries (chromedriver/node/python) are benign; a shell, osascript, or unknown wrapper parenting real 'Google Chrome' with a debugging port is suspicious. Check for a chrome_remote binary or a 'boot' process on the same host in the same window. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the Chrome + chrome_remote processes, and force-revoke/rotate browser session cookies and any SSO tokens (CDP theft is invisible to the user). 3) Hunt: pivot to all Xcode projects on the host for injected loader scripts, look for the C2 URI paths (/s/, /d/, /l, /u) in proxy logs, and check other developer endpoints that cloned the same repo.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName =~ "Google Chrome"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "--remote-debugging-port"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chromedriver","node","python","python3")
| extend UsesCustomProfile = iff(ProcessCommandLine has "--user-data-dir", "yes", "no")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, ParentProcess=InitiatingProcessFileName, ParentCmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, UsesCustomProfile, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where TargetProcessName has "Google Chrome"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "--remote-debugging-port"
| where ActingProcessName !has "chromedriver" and ActingProcessName !has "node" and ActingProcessName !has "python"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

XCSSET v40 chrome_remote backdoor execution and C2 WebSocket egress AICommand & Control High
Hunts the dropped chrome_remote Mach-O binary that XCSSET v40 uses to attach to the opened CDP port and open a persistent WebSocket to the rotating C2 for real-time JavaScript injection and cookie exfiltration. High fidelity because chrome_remote is a unique, article-named binary that should never exist on a clean macOS host. Rationale: Pivots on the article's uniquely named chrome_remote binary (the CDP-attach/WebSocket-C2 component) — a name absent from any legitimate macOS install, giving a low-FP, high-confidence signal. Corroborated by MITRE S0658 and vendor reporting describing the CDP cookie-theft backdoor. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0658/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/ • https://www.securityweek.com/new-xcsset-macos-malware-variant-hijacks-cryptocurrency-transactions/
ATT&CKT1185 T1071.001 T1539 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Extremely rare — no legitimate macOS software ships a binary named chrome_remote
  • A developer's own project artifact coincidentally named chrome_remote (check code-signing/notarization and path)
  • Security researcher detonating XCSSET samples in a lab
  • An unrelated 'Chrome Remote Desktop' component (verify full path/signature — the real one is 'chrome-remote-desktop', not 'chrome_remote')
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the chrome_remote path and SHA256, verify it is unsigned/un-notarized and dropped outside a normal app bundle; confirm whether it made outbound connections and to which host. 2) Contain: isolate the endpoint, terminate chrome_remote and its parent Chrome, block the resolved C2 IP/domain at the proxy, and invalidate all browser sessions and OAuth tokens for the user. 3) Hunt: search the fleet for the same SHA256, for Chrome launched with --remote-debugging-port (UC1), and for infected Xcode projects/loader scripts that would re-drop the binary on the next build.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName =~ "chrome_remote" or FolderPath endswith "/chrome_remote"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, ParentProcess=InitiatingProcessFileName, ParentCmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where TargetProcessName has "chrome_remote"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

XCSSET v40 build-triggered loader: Xcode build spawning osascript/curl AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the XCSSET v40 initial infection that fires only when a developer builds an infected Xcode project locally — the injected loader runs from an Xcode Run-Script build phase and spawns osascript or curl to reach the C2 and stage further modules. Article-specific because it targets the Xcode/xcodebuild build-tree ancestry that is XCSSET's signature delivery vector. Rationale: Grounded in the article's core delivery mechanic — infection triggers when the developer builds the infected Xcode project, with an AppleScript/curl loader establishing C2. Ancestry on xcodebuild/Xcode + osascript/curl is XCSSET-specific and distinct from generic script execution. Cross-checked against MITRE S0658. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0658/ • https://thehackernews.com/2025/09/new-macos-xcsset-variant-targets.html
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1059.002 T1071.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • CocoaPods / Swift Package Manager or fastlane Run-Script phases that curl dependencies during a build
  • SwiftLint / build scripts using osascript to post notifications or display dialogs
  • In-house build automation that pings a webhook via curl on build completion
  • Crashlytics/Sentry dSYM upload scripts invoking curl from a build phase
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("cocoapods","github.com","swiftpm","fastlane","crashlytics","sentry-cli"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the ProcessCommandLine of the osascript/curl child — benign build tooling references known package hosts (cocoapods.org, github.com dependency URLs); XCSSET reaches short single-letter C2 paths (/a, /s/, /d/) and base64 payloads. Inspect the offending Xcode project's build phases for an injected script. 2) Contain: quarantine the project/repo, isolate the endpoint if C2 contact is confirmed, and block the destination host. 3) Hunt: check whether Chrome was subsequently launched with --remote-debugging-port (UC1) or chrome_remote executed (UC2), and identify every other developer who cloned/built the same repo to scope worming across projects.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName in~ ("osascript","curl")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("xcodebuild","Xcode")
    or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("xcodebuild","Xcode")
    or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any (".xcodeproj",".xcworkspace","DerivedData","Build/Intermediates.noindex")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, Parent=InitiatingProcessFileName, ParentCmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, GrandParent=InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("osascript","curl")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("xcodebuild","Xcode") or ParentProcessName has_any ("xcodebuild","Xcode") or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any (".xcodeproj",".xcworkspace","DerivedData")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
